routes.description: Traditional authorship is supported by early attribution testimony considered alongside internal features connecting the texts to the named apostles or their associates.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the external traditions and internal textual features jointly make responsibility by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John more probable than late anonymous attribution.

motionBridge.description: The convergent historical evidence makes traditional responsibility for the canonical Gospels the most reasonable account.

centralBridges.description: Early, geographically distributed, substantially unanimous testimony preserves genuine information about Gospel authorship.
Internal narrative and source features fit the traditionally identified authors or authoritative eyewitness sources.
The objections from anonymity and delayed attribution do not defeat authorship when comparable ancient attribution practices are applied consistently.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The relatively less prestigious names Mark and Luke are improbable choices for an authority-enhancing fabrication.
Collaboration or educated assistance could connect a traditional source with a polished Greek literary product.

routes.description: Anonymous circulation, late naming, educational mismatch, and alternative diffusion explanations undermine identification of the canonical texts with the traditional figures.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the evidence does not reliably connect the surviving Greek texts to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John and is better explained by later attribution.

motionBridge.description: The canonical Gospels should not be attributed directly or authoritatively to the four traditional figures on the evidence presented.

centralBridges.description: Unambiguous identification of the surviving four texts occurs too late to establish continuous authorial knowledge.
The traditional apostolic figures lack the demonstrated Greek literary education required to compose the canonical narratives.
Later unanimity can arise through dependence on a common naming tradition rather than independent historical memory.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Internal features such as detailed narration or occupational vocabulary do not identify the traditional authors.
The proposed amanuensis mechanism lacks a demonstrated ancient parallel for composing extended literary narratives.

sectionJudgments.title: Early testimony and anonymous circulation
sectionJudgments.rationale: This section contains the principal affirmative external-evidence case and the negative's earliest comprehensive challenge concerning anonymity, identification, and the date of secure attribution.

proSelections.proposition: Early and geographically diverse Christian testimony consistently attributes the canonical Gospels to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, with some testimony tracing back to companions of apostles.
proSelections.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Licona the floor at event 49, and this uninterrupted opening presentation continues through event 211.

response.rationale: This is a constructive opening that advances the affirmative motion through a cumulative external-evidence route without answering an earlier selected opposing move.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move gives a developed constructive route with named witnesses, chronology, and geographic distribution.

precisionFindings.rationale: The testimony claim, its geographic scope, and its probabilistic historical function are clearly stated and expressly qualified as less than certainty.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Licona expressly treats the evidence as probabilistic, though the claimed unanimity and independence are somewhat stronger than the underlying witness relationships establish.

charity.alternative: The Gospels circulated anonymously and received their familiar names only after a substantial delay.
charity.decisiveQualification: The opposing position accepts later unanimity but disputes that it represents independent or continuous first-century knowledge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from multiple early witnesses and internal information chains to probable preservation is coherent, with independence left partly implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies numerous specific witnesses and dates, but textual identification and dependence among witnesses remain material verification questions.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The cumulative attribution argument directly supports the complete affirmative conclusion on the debate motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The anonymous-authorship alternative is acknowledged as possible and the evidence as imperfect, although its strongest dependence objection is compressed.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The sparse ledger records the survey of Papias, Justin, Irenaeus, Theophilus, the Muratorian fragment, and Clement, including dates, information chains, and regions.

conSelections.proposition: The canonical Gospels circulated without self-identification, and the first unambiguous attribution of the surviving four texts to their traditional authors appears roughly a century later.
conSelections.attributionBasis: The moderator transition and Ehrman's opening remarks identify him as the speaker, and the passage is an uninterrupted portion of his opening statement.

components.text: The cited early quotations and references do not securely identify all four surviving canonical texts by their traditional names.
The first unambiguous fourfold attribution occurs about a century after the texts had circulated anonymously.
Later unanimous titles establish what Christians eventually called the books, not what was known when they were composed.

response.rationale: Ehrman contacts the identification, chronology, and inferential significance of Licona's external witnesses and explains why delayed naming weakens the claimed preservation route.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The answer directly contests the decisive premises of the selected external-evidence case with a work-identification and chronology argument.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between anonymous circulation, unnamed quotations, and later unambiguous attribution is maintained consistently throughout the move.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Ehrman distinguishes what the record securely establishes from what remains uncertain and uses the delay to argue against, rather than logically exclude, traditional authorship.

charity.alternative: Early and geographically diverse testimony preserves accurate traditional authorship information.
charity.decisiveQualification: The affirmative relies partly on Papias and Justin as earlier links even though they do not unambiguously name all four surviving texts.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes later naming from contemporaneous authorial knowledge and consistently connects the delay to reduced evidential force.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It provides a detailed sequence of unnamed early references, disputed textual identifications, Irenaeus, and later manuscript titles.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The challenge directly attacks the affirmative motion-level inference from external testimony to traditional authorship.

representationalCharity.rationale: Ehrman concedes the reality and unanimity of later attribution while accurately isolating the disagreement over its historical significance.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The ledger records Ehrman's distinctions among anonymous texts, unnamed early quotations, uncertain Papian and Justinian identification, Irenaeus, and third-century manuscript titles.

sectionJudgments.title: Internal evidence, literacy, and Johannine authorship
sectionJudgments.rationale: This section tests the strongest internal identification claims for Luke and John against the demographic literacy objection and the Fourth Gospel's distinction between witness and authorial voice.

proSelections.proposition: The first-person plural travel narratives in Acts indicate participation by a companion of Paul, and external testimony makes Luke the most reasonable identification of that companion-author.
proSelections.attributionBasis: The passage is part of Licona's continuous opening and begins with his explicit transition from the internal evidence for Mark to Luke.

response.rationale: This constructive move develops an internal route from first-person travel narration to a Pauline companion and then uses external testimony to identify that companion as Luke.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move provides a clear constructive chain, although the transition from participant to Luke depends materially on the external tradition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly separates the participation inference from the further identification of the participant and states the conclusion as the most reasonable one.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is probabilistic and the move acknowledges that several Pauline coworkers are possible before combining the internal and external evidence.

charity.alternative: The first-person passages may be a literary device or inherited source rather than autobiographical participation by Luke.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move relies on detailed travel narration and geographic accuracy but does not independently eliminate every literary explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from first-person narration to participation is intelligible, and the separate identification step is explicit rather than conflated.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Detailed travel narration, geographic fit, and external testimony provide support, but rival explanations for first-person narration receive limited comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Identifying the common author of Luke and Acts materially advances a central affirmative bridge for one canonical Gospel.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes multiple Pauline companions but gives limited treatment to the strongest literary-source alternative.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The ledger records four shifts from third-person to first-person plural in Acts, unusually detailed travel scenes, geographic accuracy, and the external identification with Luke.

proSelections.proposition: The Fourth Gospel presents an eyewitness source identified as the beloved disciple, whose access and place among the named disciples make John son of Zebedee the best candidate.
proSelections.attributionBasis: Licona explicitly transitions to John within the same uninterrupted opening statement, with no speaker change before the passage concludes.

response.rationale: This constructive move combines the Gospel's eyewitness claims, insider detail, and elimination among a seven-disciple roster to identify John as the best candidate.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move offers a developed internal identification route, though the equation of source, beloved disciple, and final author retains an implicit bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is clear and probabilistic, but the move shifts somewhat between eyewitness source, beloved disciple, and author without fully fixing their relationship.

calibrationFindings.rationale: John is presented as the best candidate rather than a certainty, but eliminating named figures does not fully exclude an unnamed disciple or later authorial mediation.

charity.alternative: The beloved disciple supplied testimony that a separate authorial group shaped into the final Gospel.
charity.decisiveQualification: John's closing language may distinguish the witness from the collective voice that certifies and records the testimony.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The elimination argument is intelligible, but the step from an eyewitness source to John as author remains materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Precise details, Jewish knowledge, and the disciple roster are relevant, while identification of the beloved disciple and final writer remains underdetermined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central internal-evidence route for traditional responsibility for the Fourth Gospel.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes that the beloved disciple may be the source, but it does not fully develop the strongest distinction between source and final author.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The ledger records exact times, incidental details, Jewish insider knowledge, eyewitness language, John 21's roster, and elimination of Peter and James.

conSelections.proposition: Galilean disciples lacking elite Greek literary education could not plausibly have composed the sophisticated Greek narratives preserved as the canonical Gospels.
conSelections.attributionBasis: The passage remains in Ehrman's uninterrupted opening statement and is introduced as his most important consideration about the authors' identities.

components.text: John is presented in Acts as unlettered, while composing the Gospel required prolonged elite Greek literary education.
Internal participation clues do not by themselves demonstrate that the traditionally named figure possessed the education required for final literary composition.

response.rationale: The move supplies a general demographic and educational objection that decisively contacts direct Johannine composition, while its contact with the Luke argument is less specific because Luke's background is uncertain.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The decisive capacity objection strongly contacts John but only partially addresses the separate inference identifying the Acts traveler as Luke.

precisionFindings.rationale: The education requirement is clear, but the conclusion sometimes generalizes from Galilean disciples to Mark and Luke despite conceding limited biographical knowledge about them.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The evidence strongly lowers the probability of direct apostolic composition, but categorical inability for all four traditional figures exceeds the individualized evidence supplied.

charity.alternative: Traditional figures could be sources or responsible authors working through educated collaborators.
charity.decisiveQualification: The motion includes writing under a figure's authority, while the literacy evidence most directly defeats unaided personal composition.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The education-to-capacity inference is coherent, but its extension across all four named figures and authority-mediated authorship is not fully secured.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies extensive demographic, educational, literacy, geographic, and textual evidence, including Acts' description of John as unlettered.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The claimed mismatch directly attacks traditional composition at the motion level, though it is less complete against mediated authority.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move engages the collaboration alternative but tends to describe the affirmative conclusion as direct composition more broadly than Licona's qualified Matthew theory.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The ledger contains a sustained review of ancient wealth, education stages, literacy rates, rural Galilee, composition training, and Acts 4:13.

conSelections.proposition: Later authorship witnesses are not independent once a naming tradition begins, and John's closing distinction between the beloved disciple and a collective authorial voice weighs against direct Johannine authorship.
conSelections.attributionBasis: Licona's rebuttal ends before this response, and the moderator's transition plus the first-person counterargument clearly identify Ehrman as speaker.

components.text: The closing formulation distinguishes the disciple who testified from the collective voice saying that his testimony is true.
Detailed knowledge about a character does not itself identify that character as the writer of the narrative.

response.rationale: The reply directly attacks both the inference from intimate detail and the equation of the beloved disciple's testimony with authorship of the final Gospel.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move explicitly contacts the two decisive internal steps and states why each fails to establish direct Johannine authorship.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes later witness dependence from the separate internal distinction between an eyewitness source and final author.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The language is used as evidence weighing against direct authorship rather than as categorical proof that John supplied no testimony.

charity.alternative: John 21 identifies the beloved disciple as both witness and writer, with a community endorsing his testimony.
charity.decisiveQualification: The affirmative can read the third person as self-reference, but the collective certification still permits a separate final voice.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between testimony and final authorial voice is clearly drawn and directly undermines the affirmative's compressed identity step.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The textual wording supplies concrete support, though the grammatical dispute permits an alternative reading in which the disciple wrote underlying material.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks a central internal bridge for traditional Johannine authorship.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move represents the affirmative textual inference accurately and challenges its decisive qualification rather than denying possible eyewitness input.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The ledger records Ehrman's analysis of John 21's wording, the collective certification of the disciple's testimony, and the analogy distinguishing a witness from a reporter.

sectionJudgments.title: Ancient parallels, Papias, and collaborative composition
sectionJudgments.rationale: This section captures the strongest direct rebuttal exchange over anonymity, comparative ancient attribution, Papias, Justin, and the proposed mechanism of literate assistance.

proSelections.proposition: Anonymous composition and delayed explicit attribution do not defeat traditional authorship because comparable ancient works are accepted on similarly late testimony, while Papias and Justin provide earlier support for Mark.
proSelections.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly awards Licona the first rebuttal at event 395, and Licona identifies the opposing claims he is reviewing throughout this passage.

components.text: Lack of embedded author names was ordinary for surviving ancient biographies and therefore is not independently disqualifying.
Other accepted ancient works receive explicit attribution only from comparably or substantially later testimony.
Papias and Justin provide earlier evidence connecting Mark's Gospel with Peter before Irenaeus's fourfold naming.

response.rationale: Licona directly answers the anonymity, lateness, and lack-of-earlier-identification components by invoking genre practice, classical comparisons, and earlier Mark-related witnesses.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move contacts every decisive component of the selected lateness challenge, though the comparators and Justin identification require further defense.

precisionFindings.rationale: The response clearly distinguishes internal anonymity from historical attribution and limits its strongest early-identification claim principally to Mark.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The response reasonably shows that anonymity and delay are not decisive alone, but compatibility with other ancient cases does not itself establish Gospel authorship.

charity.alternative: The delayed and ambiguous early record makes the traditional attributions historically weak or invented.
charity.decisiveQualification: Ehrman's claim concerns work-specific evidence, not a rule that all anonymously transmitted ancient works lack authors.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The rebuttal coherently weakens the inference from anonymity and delay, though the comparative argument cannot independently prove traditional attribution.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific classical cases, biographical practice, Papias, and Justin are offered, but their comparability and textual identification remain contested.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly defends the central external-evidence route against the negative's principal objections.

representationalCharity.rationale: Licona acknowledges Ehrman's chronology and anonymity points but sometimes compresses the demand for work-specific evidence into generalized skepticism.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The ledger records the survey of anonymous biographies, delayed attribution of classical works, Papias's Mark report, and Justin's uniquely Markan sons-of-thunder material.

conSelections.proposition: Classical parallels do not establish Gospel authorship, Papias is an unreliable and selectively used witness, and the proposed use of literate assistants lacks ancient evidence.
conSelections.attributionBasis: A clear speaker transition follows Licona's rebuttal conclusion, and the new speaker explicitly addresses Mike's arguments from the preceding presentation.

components.text: Late attribution of other works is probative only if the work-specific evidence establishing those attributions is shown to be comparable.
Papias is selectively trusted for Mark despite uncertain identification and traditions that raise substantial reliability concerns.
No ancient evidence was supplied for an assistant composing an extended sophisticated narrative under an illiterate disciple's authority.

response.rationale: Ehrman answers the comparator, Papias, and collaboration defenses by demanding case-specific warrants and identifying the absence of an analogous narrative-composition practice.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply explicitly contacts the decisive warrant behind each major defense and states why each fails to carry the authorship inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The response consistently distinguishes simple dictation or attribution from composition of a sustained literary narrative in another person's name.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The demand for an ancient parallel is well framed, but statements that no such practice existed are stronger than the necessarily incomplete surviving record permits.

charity.alternative: Anonymous ancient biography, Papias, Justin, and literate assistance jointly preserve a plausible traditional-authorship route.
charity.decisiveQualification: The affirmative presents collaboration as historical plausibility rather than claiming a surviving contract or named secretary.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response consistently separates generic compatibility from work-specific evidence and applies that distinction across the proposed defenses.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move supplies concrete counterexamples, Papian material, and a claimed survey of secretarial references, though the universal negative remains difficult to establish.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the affirmative's central comparative and testimonial defense of traditional authorship.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately identifies the affirmative mechanisms, with slight overcompression of collaboration into full ghostwriting.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The ledger records the demand for work-specific classical evidence, challenges concerning Justin and Papias, Papias's unusual traditions, and the survey of ancient secretarial practices.

sectionJudgments.title: Why the traditional names were chosen
sectionJudgments.rationale: This compact exchange tests a decisive explanatory prediction of the late-naming hypothesis: whether Mark and Luke are implausibly weak fabricated names or strategically useful apostolic associates.

proSelections.proposition: Christians inventing prestigious gospel attributions would not plausibly have selected the comparatively less marketable Mark and Luke instead of direct disciples.
proSelections.attributionBasis: The moderator-designated questioning sequence and the explicit turn-taking make Licona's identity as the speaker unambiguous.

components.text: A deliberate authority-enhancing fabrication predicts direct apostolic names more naturally than the comparatively minor Mark and Luke.

response.rationale: The move challenges the causal adequacy of later invented attribution by identifying a naming choice that appears surprising under a simple prestige-maximization account.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive implication of the later-naming hypothesis but does not address the full chronology or diffusion case.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is framed as a comparative plausibility challenge and clearly identifies Mark and Luke as the allegedly surprising choices.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The naming choice creates a legitimate puzzle, but it assumes that direct personal prestige was the only or dominant attribution strategy.

charity.alternative: The names were chosen to connect the four Gospels collectively with the leading apostolic witnesses.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mark and Luke may be less famous personally while remaining valuable as associates of Peter and Paul.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The prediction from an authority-enhancing motive to more prestigious names is coherent but depends on a simplified model of the fabricators' aims.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The observed names support the challenge, but no broader base rate of invented attributions or competing motives is developed in this short exchange.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks a central causal explanation for late traditional attribution.

representationalCharity.rationale: It captures the authority motive but initially omits the stronger collective-apostolic-witness rationale for Mark and Luke.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The ledger records Licona's contrast between Mark and Luke and more obviously marketable apostolic names used in later apocryphal works.

conSelections.proposition: Mark and Luke were useful attribution choices because they were understood as companions of Peter and Paul, completing a representation of the principal apostolic witness.
conSelections.attributionBasis: The moderator invites an answer immediately after Licona's question, and the content is Ehrman's direct response within his established turn.

components.text: Mark and Luke carried derivative authority through Peter and Paul despite not being direct disciples of Jesus.
Two disciples plus companions of the two leading apostles form a coherent representation of the wider apostolic witness.

response.rationale: Ehrman directly answers why apparently minor names could serve an authority-enhancing attribution strategy and supplies a concrete four-name pattern rather than a bare motive assertion.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response contacts the precise surprise identified by Licona and gives a concise alternative that neutralizes its decisive premise.

precisionFindings.rationale: The relationships among Mark, Luke, Peter, Paul, and the two direct disciples are stated clearly without shifting the scope of the claim.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move offers a plausible motive and structural explanation rather than claiming documentary certainty about the namers' intentions.

charity.alternative: Fabricators seeking authority would have selected only famous direct eyewitnesses.
charity.decisiveQualification: The four-name scheme can seek comprehensive apostolic coverage rather than maximize each individual name's independent prestige.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response provides a clear and economical explanation of why the two associate names remain useful under the late-attribution hypothesis.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The known traditional associations with Peter and Paul support the explanation, though the namers' actual deliberations remain reconstructive.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The answer materially supports the central alternative explanation for the traditional fourfold naming pattern.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response directly adopts the strongest version of Licona's objection and answers the precise concern about relative prestige.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The ledger records Ehrman's appeal to Mark as Peter's companion and Luke as Paul's companion, alongside Matthew and John as direct disciples.

sectionJudgments.title: Competing explanations of later unanimity
sectionJudgments.rationale: The closing exchange integrates the external and internal cases and directly tests whether geographic unanimity reflects independent early memory or diffusion from a common late-second-century source.

proSelections.proposition: Geographically broad and uncontested early testimony, reinforced by compatible internal features and consistent treatment of ancient literature, makes traditional Gospel authorship the most reasonable explanation.
proSelections.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Licona's closing statement, which proceeds continuously through the end of this passage without a competing speaker.

components.text: Geographically broad agreement without surviving rival attributions is presented as positive evidence rather than merely a late label.
Compatible internal features are combined with external testimony rather than treated as standalone proof of identity.
The same historical standards applied to other ancient literature are claimed to leave the Gospel attributions comparatively credible.
Mark's relative obscurity is retained as evidence against a straightforward prestige-maximizing invention.
The closing relies on the previously proposed involvement and assistance model but does not newly substantiate its historical mechanism.

response.rationale: The closing synthesizes the affirmative evidence and directly contests late convergence, but it does not fully answer the selected literacy and extended-composition objection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move contacts several decisive objections strongly while leaving the literacy and collaboration mechanism materially underanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The closing consistently states a most-reasonable-explanation conclusion, distinguishes fit from proof, and expressly acknowledges reasonable doubt.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is carefully probabilistic, though it treats geographic testimony as more independent and early than the negative's diffusion evidence permits without further support.

charity.alternative: A common late naming origin spread the same four attributions across already authoritative anonymous texts.
charity.decisiveQualification: The negative alternative offers a specific Roman diffusion mechanism rather than requiring wholly independent simultaneous invention across regions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cumulative inference is clear and the evidence categories are integrated, but independence and collaboration remain important unresolved bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The closing draws on substantial earlier evidence, while its strongest claims about independence, ancient silence, and comparative parity remain contested.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The integrated conclusion directly supports the complete affirmative motion and identifies the proposed best explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The closing accurately identifies anonymous late attribution but describes the alternative too often as unsupported convergence despite the articulated diffusion model.

proSelections.evidenceBasis: The ledger records the closing synthesis of six witnesses, geographic distribution, absence of rival names, internal fit, minor-name reasoning, and comparative historical practice.

conSelections.proposition: Universal use of the four names after the late second century can derive from a common Roman naming origin and therefore does not establish that the names accompanied the Gospels from composition.
conSelections.attributionBasis: This passage begins Ehrman's closing statement after Licona finishes, and its sustained first-person response is clearly attributed to him.

components.text: Universal testimony after the names became established does not demonstrate what the books were called during their earlier anonymous circulation.
Irenaeus and the Muratorian fragment can be connected with Rome at the same late-second-century stage, supplying a common point of diffusion.
A tradition originating at one influential center can subsequently become geographically universal without independent invention in every region.

response.rationale: The closing reply directly answers the affirmative's strongest inference from geographic unanimity by supplying a temporally and geographically specific dependence model.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The response targets the decisive independence premise and explains exactly how the same later names could spread without accompanying original composition.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move distinguishes pre-naming silence, the late-second-century naming event, and subsequent geographic diffusion with stable chronological scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The Roman-origin account is presented as a sufficient alternative explanation rather than as a documented certainty about the exact naming event.

charity.alternative: Geographically diverse unanimous testimony is best explained by authentic attribution accompanying the Gospels from their early circulation.
charity.decisiveQualification: The affirmative evidence becomes geographically broad after the point at which dependence on a common naming tradition is possible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The common-source diffusion model directly explains the observed later unanimity without contradicting the earlier anonymous record.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The timing and Roman associations of the earliest fourfold witnesses support the model, though the precise act of naming remains inferential.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the central external bridge rather than every component of the complete motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: Ehrman concedes the later unanimity and geographic spread, then disputes only the inference drawn from those accepted facts.

conSelections.evidenceBasis: The ledger records the late-second-century timing, the Roman associations of Irenaeus and the Muratorian fragment, Justin's earlier failure to use the names, and the diffusion analogy.
